metadata.title: Why Tesla-SpaceX Merger Talks Face ‘More Friction Than People Assume’

content.text:
Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.
Elon Musk's Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) and SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) are racing to agree on the terms of a $3.5 trillion merger before the end of the year, but negotiations are proving harder than expected.
"There is more friction than people assume," a person familiar with the negotiations told the Financial Times on Tuesday. The source said the two sides were not yet close to an agreement, although a year-end deal remained possible.
Five directors are negotiating through two special committees, three representing Tesla and two representing SpaceX. Musk, who runs both companies, cannot formally participate in negotiations.
"It's sort of an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can't be in the conversation," Musk said in October.
Why Tesla Is Being More Careful
SpaceX's directors are reportedly more comfortable with Musk's ambitions. Tesla's are thinking about the courtroom.
"They know there will be lawsuits. Every text message and email will come out," a person involved in the negotiations told the FT.
Tesla has been here before. Its 2016 acquisition of SolarCity triggered years of litigation after shareholders alleged Musk had engineered the transaction to rescue another company in which he held a substantial stake.
The Delaware Supreme Court ultimately upheld the acquisition, but a person familiar with the talks told Reuters in October that the case could become a reference point if the committees are not adequately insulated from Musk's influence.
Central to the negotiations is the exchange ratio. Under the proposed all-stock merger, the relative valuations of the two companies will determine how much of the combined business each set of shareholders receives.
Musk owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and just under half of SpaceX, giving him a greater financial interest in a higher SpaceX valuation. Tesla's directors will need to demonstrate that this conflict did not compromise the deal for their shareholders.
Prediction Traders See A Longer Timeline
Musk biographer Walter Isaacson said earlier this month it was "almost inconceivable" that the companies would not eventually merge.
Prediction traders largely agree, but remain skeptical of the year-end target.
Traders on Polymarket put the probability of an official merger announcement by Dec. 31 at 36%, rising to 62% by the end of January and 87% by the end of 2027.
The pricing suggests traders see a delay as more likely than the talks collapsing. The market has attracted $1.87 million in trading volume.
